summary:
EmberEye is an open source web app that utilises various NASA datasets to harmonize 20+ years of satellite fire data, compare fire seasons against history, and simulate how fires might spread. It’s free and accessible, where users simply choose an area and dates. EmberEye also uses NASA weather, dryness and terrain data to power a fire activity outlook map, showing where fire is more likely than usual each month.

We are Indonesians who live in Australia, where fires are close to both of our homes. This inspired us to support the combat against wildfires, helping responders and researchers quickly identify unusual fire seasons and where fire may spread next.

The two satellite sensors MODIS and VIIRS perceive fires differently. MODIS has recorded fires since 2002 but detects fewer of them, whereas VIIRS, which joined in 2012, detects about 4 times more fire due to its higher resolution. EmberEye harmonizes this data so that MODIS matches VIIRS. When tested on hidden years, monthly totals were off by only 2.2% on average, compared with 77% for the raw data.

EmberEye is built from our own experience of fire, for anyone who needs to understand it.
details:
NASA satellites have recorded fire hotspots for more than twenty years, so a question like "is this fire season unusual?" should be easy to answer. The catch is that the record changes partway through. MODIS has watched since 2002 at about 1 km, and VIIRS joined in 2012 at 375 m. VIIRS picks up smaller fires, so raw counts jump about four times overnight, and 2012 looks like the year the world caught fire. EmberEye puts the whole record on one scale and turns it into a tool anyone can use. So, we count "fire cell-days" instead of dots. Each hexagon of ground, about 0.7 km², that burned on a given day counts once, whichever satellite saw it. From 2012 to 2019, both satellites were watching the same fires, so we used those years to measure the VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio for each region and month (about 4.2 worldwide). We then scaled the older years to match. When Suomi NPP stopped sending data on 2 November 2026, we carried the record on with NOAA-20. To test it, we calibrated on 2012 to 2016 and predicted 2017 to 2019 from MODIS alone. Worldwide monthly totals were off by 2.2% on average compared with what VIIRS actually saw. Raw MODIS was off by 77%.

What it does Pick any area on Earth and a date range. A burning calendar shows every month from 2002 to 2026, either as counts or compared with that place's usual level. You can play a season on the map, see fire intensity, weather and the Fire Weather Index, and download the hotspots as CSV. It's free, needs no login and works on a phone. Beyond the brief, we added a fire-spread simulation: start a fire anywhere and see how it might spread, always labelled as an estimate. There's also a fire activity outlook showing where fire is more likely than usual this month, which is not an official fire danger rating. Who it's for Emergency responders, researchers, land managers and firefighters who need to know whether what they're seeing is normal for that place and time of year. Agricultural and land-clearing burns are included on purpose. How we built it Data pipeline: Python with DuckDB and the H3 hexagon grid. API: FastAPI and DuckDB on Vercel, with hotspot data stored in Cloudflare R2. Site and dashboard: Astro, React and TypeScript, with MapLibre and deck.gl for the map. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), MERRA-2, GFWED, MODIS land cover, SRTM and GIBS, plus OpenStreetMap and Natural Earth. What we kept in mind Honesty about the data: the app always says whether something is observed, harmonized or simulated, and lists its limits.

AI Usage

Tool: Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant running in our editor and terminal. Both team members used it.

How we used it: we described what we wanted and reviewed what it produced. It wrote and edited code, ran our scripts and tests, and helped find and fix bugs. We tested features ourselves on the local and live site and asked for changes until they worked the way we wanted.

Where:

  • Data pipeline (pipeline/): cleaning and harmonizing the FIRMS records, the holdout validation (validate.py), weather, Fire Weather Index and land cover processing, the simulation input tiles and the home page hero map (hero_map/).
  • API (api/): the FastAPI + DuckDB routes (calendar, hotspots, stats, exports, risk outlook, simulation tiles) and performance work (sampled files, caching).
  • Dashboard (web/): map layers, burning calendar, stats charts, downloads and the "Download all" ZIP, share links, the fire-spread simulation model and the risk outlook.
  • Home page and docs: the home page, its design and animations, the README and in-app text.

What the team did: chose the approach and features, found and downloaded the NASA datasets, made the design and data decisions, tested everything, and reviewed and approved all changes. Every number shown, such as the validation results, comes from running our code on NASA data.

What AI did not do: no data was generated by AI. Hotspots, weather and fire activity come from the NASA datasets listed above, and simulated fire spread is clearly labelled as an estimate.

We also used Claude (claude.ai) for planning, research and drafting the presentation and submission text.

Accessibility: Colour-blind-safe colours, keyboard support and reduced motion.

Cost: Keeping it fast and free to run.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/DarylWiriadi/EmberEye
